title: Family: kinds of family, relatives and sharing the work
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers NCERT Class 3 'Family and Friends' (members of a family, how they are related, how they support each other, the joy of living together) and NIOS Class 3 Lesson 1 'Concept of Family and Interpersonal Relations' (the family, relations, parents' responsibility to children, status of girls and women), plus kinship, inheritance, shared ancestry and families in other animals. No textbook needed.
summary: Families come in many shapes, and what they share is care. Your child learns the Indian names for relatives, builds a family tree, and sorts which features run in the family and which are learned. They find out that, far enough back, every person's family tree joins everyone else's. They meet elephant families led by grandmothers, find out that human children have always been raised by many hands, count who does the work at home, think about fairness for girls and boys, play the games their grandparents played, and make something to say 'I love you'.
builds_on: This is the first rung on family. Later rungs on growing up and having young, genes and inheriting features, and society and community build on it: how traits are passed on, how communities support families, and the rights of children.
subconcepts: what a family is: people who belong to and care for each other
many shapes of family: nuclear, joint, single-parent, adoptive, foster, raised by grandparents
relations and kinship words: Indian languages name the father's side and the mother's side
family resemblance: some features are passed on through genes, others are learned
everyone's family tree joins: all humans share ancestors
families in other animals: elephant herds led by grandmothers
it takes many hands: humans as cooperative breeders
sharing the work at home: paid and unpaid care work
what parents and guardians owe children: children's rights
girls and boys are equal in the family
caring for elders and family members with disabilities
the joy of living together: games, stories and love across generations
chosen family: friends and neighbours who become family
goals: By the end your child can describe several shapes of family and say what all of them share.
By the end your child can draw their family tree across three generations and use the right kinship words.
By the end your child can sort features into those passed on in the family and those learned, and explain why many are both.
By the end your child can explain why every person's family tree, followed far enough back, joins everyone else's.
By the end your child can name who does the work at home, and explain why girls and boys should share it and have the same rights.
By the end your child can describe how elephants and humans raise their young with help from many family members.
words: family
people who belong to each other and care for each other
relative
a person in your family, near or far
generation
all the people in a family who are about the same age, like you and your cousins
ancestor
a person in your family who lived long before you: a great-great-grandparent and further back
joint family
a family where grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts and children live together
nuclear family
a family of parents (or one parent) and their children living together
adoption
when a child legally becomes the child of a family they were not born into
trait
a feature, like curly hair or dimples
gene
a tiny instruction inside our cells, passed from parents to children, that helps shape some traits
matriarch
the oldest female who leads a family, like a grandmother elephant
unpaid work
work done for the family, like cooking, cleaning and caring, that nobody is paid for
right
something every person should have, which no one should take away

days.title: Who is my family?
days.goal: Make a family handprint, meet the story, and see that families come in many shapes.

steps.title: The family handprint
steps.do: Spread a large sheet of paper on the floor. Each person at home (and anyone who visits this week) presses a hand in poster paint onto the paper, overlapping a little, and writes their name next to it. Add a small paw print for a pet if you have one, and draw outlines for family who live far away. Ask: 'Are any two handprints the same?' (No: different sizes, lines and fingers.) 'What do they make together?' Keep the sheet: it is the cover of the family book project. Also start the chore survey (experiment e3) today: stick the chart on the fridge.

steps.title: Story: Where My Tree Begins
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Don't explain it. Ask: 'Why did Tara think her tree had no roots? What did Kavya Akka show her?' Write down your child's answer to the second question; you will come back to it on Day 4.

steps.title: Many shapes of family
steps.do: Ask: 'Who lives in your home? Who is family but lives somewhere else?' Then describe these families and ask, for each, 'Is this a family?': Anjali lives with her Amma, Appa, Paati, Thatha, her uncle, aunt and two cousins (a joint family). Joseph lives with his Pappa and his little sister (a single-parent family). Lakshmi was adopted as a baby by her two parents. Karthik and his brother live with their Ammamma, their mother's mother, who looks after them. Irfan lives with a foster family while his own mother is in hospital. Good answer: all are families. Ask: 'So what makes a family a family?' Listen for: caring for each other, belonging, being there. Say: 'Families come in many shapes. What they share is care.'

steps.title: Draw your family your way
steps.do: Your child draws their family in any way they like: as people, as animals, as trees, as a house with windows. Say: 'There's no right way.' Ask: 'Who did you put closest to you? Why? Who did you nearly forget?' Don't correct anything; just listen.

need: the chore survey chart (see experiment e3)

days.title: A name for every relation
days.goal: Learn kinship words and build a three-generation family tree.

steps.title: Words for uncle and aunty
steps.do: Ask: 'In English, what do you call your father's brother? Your mother's brother? Your mother's sister's husband?' (All 'uncle'.) Then ask: 'What do we call them at home?' Make a table with your child. Father's brother: Tamil chithappa (younger) or periyappa (elder), Kannada chikkappa or doddappa, Telugu babai or pedananna, Hindi chacha or tau, Bengali kaka or jethu. Mother's brother: Tamil maama, Telugu mavayya, Kannada maava, Hindi and Bengali mama. Father's sister: Tamil athai, Kannada atte, Telugu atta, Hindi bua, Bengali pishi. Mother's sister: Tamil chithi or periyamma, Telugu pinni or pedamma, Kannada chikkamma or doddamma, Hindi mausi, Bengali mashi. Ask: 'Why do you think Indian languages have so many more words?' Good ideas: big joint families; it matters which side of the family someone is from; different relatives have different roles. Say: 'Words show what a people care about.'

steps.title: Our family tree
steps.do: Do activity a1. Draw a tree on a big sheet: your child at the trunk, parents on the first branches, grandparents above, and great-grandparents at the top if anyone knows their names. Add brothers, sisters and cousins on their own branches. Write each person's kinship word, birthplace and one thing they love. Phone a grandparent or elder to fill gaps. Ask: 'How many generations does our tree have? Where did each generation grow up?'

steps.title: Generations
steps.do: Point along the tree. Say: 'Each row is a generation: you and your cousins are one generation, your parents and their brothers and sisters are the next, your grandparents the next.' Ask: 'Which generation do you think saw the biggest changes in their life?' Keep the question for Day 7's interview.

need: a big sheet of paper or chart
a phone to call an elder

days.title: Whose nose? Traits in the family
days.goal: Compare features across the family, and separate what is passed on from what is learned.

steps.title: The family trait survey
steps.do: Do experiment e1. With the family (and photos of grandparents), fill in the table for each person: curly or straight hair, dimples, eye colour, left- or right-handed, height, which language they spoke first, a favourite food, a way of laughing. Ask: 'Which features show up in more than one generation? Which ones doesn't anyone else have?' Then sort the features into three groups: mostly passed on through the body (hair type, eye colour, dimples), mostly learned (language, favourite food, songs), and both (height, which also depends on food and health; a way of laughing, which you may pick up from people you live with).

steps.title: Genes and learning
steps.do: Say: 'Inside every cell of your body are tiny instructions called genes. You got half from your birth mother and half from your birth father, mixed up in a new way. That's why you can have your mother's hair and your father's ears, but no one is a copy.' Ask: 'If a child is adopted, which features might be like their new family?' Good answer: language, way of talking, favourite foods, songs, jokes, values, even ways of walking or laughing, all learned by living together. Say: 'A family passes on two kinds of things: genes, and everything you learn by living together. Both make you you.'

steps.title: Swap places
steps.do: Play a short drama. Your child becomes a parent or grandparent for three minutes, and you become your child. Act a real scene: getting everyone ready in the morning, or a child who won't eat their vegetables. Then swap back. Ask: 'What did it feel like to be Amma? What was hard? What did you notice that you never noticed before?' Then ask: 'What is the same about you and Amma? You and Thatha?'

need: photos of grandparents and great-grandparents if you have them

days.title: All our family trees join
days.goal: Discover that ancestors double each generation, so everyone's family trees join.

steps.title: Doubling ancestors
steps.do: Do experiment e2. Put one rice grain for your child. Two grains for parents, four for grandparents, eight for great-grandparents, then sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four. Your child counts the grains for each generation and writes the numbers. Then use a calculator together to keep doubling up to 30 generations (about 750 years). Ask: 'How many ancestors at 30 generations?' (More than one billion.) 'But there were far fewer than a billion people in the world 750 years ago. How can that be?'

steps.title: The trees that join
steps.do: Help your child see the answer: 'Many of those billion places are filled by the same people. Your great-great-grandmother on your mother's side may also be your great-great-great-grandmother on your father's side, if your families married into the same village long ago. Go back far enough and the family trees of everyone on Earth run into each other.' Draw two family trees side by side whose top branches meet in the same few people. Go back to the story: 'Was Tara right that her tree had no roots?' Ask: 'If you go back far enough, who is in your family?'

steps.title: How far back to everyone?
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v1: the mathematicians who used computer models to work out how many generations back the family trees of all living humans meet. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Cousins beyond humans
steps.do: Show your child pictures of a monkey and a tree. Ask: 'What do you share with each?' Good answers: a monkey has hands, a mother and a family. A tree is alive, grows and is made of cells, like us. Say: 'Humans and monkeys share ancestors who lived millions of years ago. Scientists have found that, far enough back, all living things share ancestors, even you and a tree.'

need: pictures of a monkey and a tree

days.title: Elephant aunts and many hands
days.goal: See how elephants and humans raise their young together.

steps.title: Families led by grandmothers
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v2: Cynthia Moss, who has watched the same elephant families in Amboseli, Kenya, for over fifty years, and found that elephant families are led by the oldest female, the matriarch, whose memory helps everyone survive. Say: 'Young elephants are looked after by their mothers, and also by aunts, big sisters and cousins, who are called allomothers.' Ask the voice question.

steps.title: It takes many hands
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v3: Sarah Blaffer Hrdy's idea that human babies have always needed many people, not just a mother, to raise them. Ask the voice question. Then point out other animals that raise young together: meerkats, wolves, some birds like jungle babblers in India, where older brothers and sisters help feed the chicks.

steps.title: Who helped raise me?
steps.do: Ask your child to list everyone who has helped look after them since they were born: parents, grandparents, aunts, older cousins, an akka or didi who looked after them, a neighbour aunty, a teacher, a doctor, the vaccinator at the health centre. Write the list. Ask: 'How many hands? What would have happened if only one person had done it all?'

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws1. Your child reads and answers; help with reading only if needed. Check together.

need: pictures of elephants if you have them

days.title: Who does the work? Fair for everyone
days.goal: Look at the chore survey results, think about unpaid work, and learn what children are owed.

steps.title: Chore survey results
steps.do: Look at the chore chart from experiment e3, kept since Day 1. Add up the minutes or ticks for each person: cooking, washing up, sweeping, washing clothes, shopping, caring for children or elders, paid work outside. Make a bar chart. Ask: 'Who does the most work in our home? Who does the least? Is the work shared fairly? Which work did we forget to count?' (Often: planning meals, remembering everyone's needs, comforting someone.) Don't blame anyone; just notice.

steps.title: Work that nobody counts
steps.do: Tell your child about voice v4: Marilyn Waring, who pointed out that the cooking, cleaning and caring done at home is not counted when countries measure their work. Say: 'In India, a government survey in 2019 found that women spend about five hours a day on unpaid housework and care, and men about one and a half hours.' Ask the voice question. Ask: 'What is one job at home that you could do every day from now on?'

steps.title: What every child is owed
steps.do: Ask: 'What do parents or guardians have to give a child?' Make a list together: food, a safe home, love, health care and vaccinations, schooling, time to play, being listened to, protection from harm. Say: 'These are called children's rights. In 1989 the countries of the world wrote them down together, and almost every country has agreed to them. India's law says every child aged 6 to 14 has the right to free schooling.' Then ask: 'Should girls and boys in a family get the same food, the same schooling, the same chores and the same chances?' (Yes.) Say gently: 'In some families, girls have been given less: less food, less school, more chores. Indian law now says daughters and sons must get the same chance at school, and for most families the same share of the family's property. Fairness starts at home.' Ask: 'Is anything in our home different for girls and boys? Should it be?'

days.title: Games our grandparents played
days.goal: Play old games with elders, interview them about then and now, and think about caring for elders.

steps.title: Play the old games
steps.do: Ask a grandparent or elder (in person or on a video call) to teach a game they played as a child: pallanguzhi (a board of 14 pits and seeds or shells), nondi or stapu (hopscotch), gilli-danda, kho-kho, pithoo (lagori, with seven flat stones and a ball), chaupar, or a clapping game. Make the board or court together from what you have: draw pallanguzhi pits on paper and use tamarind seeds; draw a nondi court on the floor with chalk. Play at least two rounds. Ask: 'What do you need to win? Is it luck, or skill, or both?'

steps.title: Then-and-now interview
steps.do: Do activity a2. Your child interviews the elder with these questions, and writes or records the answers: 'Where did you grow up? How many people lived in your home? What did you eat? How did you go to school? What did children do to help at home? What is better now? What was better then?' At the end your child asks: 'What is one thing you want me to remember?'

steps.title: Caring for each other
steps.do: Ask: 'When you were a baby, the family looked after you. Who looks after the elders now?' Talk about what elders may need: help with walking or eyesight, someone to talk to, medicines on time, patience. Ask: 'If someone in the family can't see, hear or walk, how can everyone make home easier for them?' (Keep things in the same place, speak clearly and face them, ramps, learning some sign language.) Say: 'Caring flows both ways and changes over a lifetime.'

need: a grandparent or elder (in person or on a call)
paper and a pencil or a phone to record

days.title: Chosen family and saying I love you
days.goal: Think about friends and neighbours who become family, make cards, and play the game.

steps.title: Handmade cards
steps.do: Your child makes two handmade cards: one for someone in the family, and one for someone who is 'like family' but not related: a best friend, a neighbour, a teacher, the akka or didi who looked after them. Fold paper, decorate it with drawings, a small kolam pattern or leaf prints, and write one thing they love about that person. Ask: 'Why is this person like family to you?' Deliver the cards today if you can.

steps.title: Relation Rummy card game
steps.do: Play the card game g1. Read the rules aloud. When a player lays a set, they must say the relation in at least two Indian languages, or in the language your family speaks.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws2. Your child works alone. For the written items, ask them to read their answer aloud and then ask: 'Can you think of a family where that would be different?'

days.title: Our family book, check and teach it back
days.goal: Finish the family book, tackle the challenge sheet and teach the family.

steps.title: Finish the family book
steps.do: Put the family book together: the handprint cover (Day 1), the family tree (Day 2), the trait table (Day 3), the doubling ancestors numbers (Day 4), the 'who helped raise me' list (Day 5), the chore bar chart (Day 6) and the elder's interview (Day 7). Staple or tie with string.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3. These are thinking questions; there may be more than one good answer. Ask your child to explain their reasons aloud before writing.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child presents the family book to the family, explaining: the shapes families come in, the kinship words, what is passed on and what is learned, why all family trees join, how elephants and humans raise young with many hands, and what the chore survey showed. Then ask the check questions. End by asking everyone at home: 'What is one thing you learned about our family this week?'

experiments.title: The family trait survey
experiments.question: Which features run in families, and which are learned?
need: a table with columns: name, generation, hair, dimples, eye colour, left or right handed, height, first language, favourite food, way of laughing
steps: Fill in the table for everyone at home.
Use photos or a phone call to add grandparents and great-grandparents.
Circle any feature that appears in two or more generations.
Sort the features into: mostly passed on through genes, mostly learned, or both.
Write one surprising thing you found.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which feature do you think you got from whom?'
experiments.observe: Some features (hair type, dimples, eye colour) often show up across generations; others (language, recipes, songs) are shared because people learn them together. Many (height, ways of talking) are a mixture.
experiments.why: Children get half their genes from each birth parent, in a new mix, so they share some features with each parent but are never a copy. Most features are shaped by many genes and also by food, health and surroundings. A great deal of what makes a family feel like a family (language, humour, values, food) is learned by living together, which is why adopted children share so much with their families.
experiments.safety: Be gentle: in adoptive, foster or blended families, focus on learned traits and let the child choose what to share.

experiments.title: Doubling ancestors
experiments.question: How many ancestors do you have, and why do family trees join?
steps: Put 1 grain for you.
Put 2 grains for your parents, 4 for grandparents, 8 for great-grandparents, 16, 32, then 64.
Write the numbers in a column.
With a calculator, keep doubling to 30 generations.
Each generation is about 25 years. Work out how many years back 30 generations is (about 750 years).
experiments.predict: Ask: 'How many ancestors do you think you had 30 generations ago?'
experiments.observe: The numbers grow very fast: 64 at 6 generations, over 1,000 at 10, over a billion at 30.
experiments.why: Each person has two parents, so the number of places in a family tree doubles every generation. But 750 years ago there were only a few hundred million people in the whole world, so the same ancestors must fill many places in everyone's tree. Family trees overlap and join, until, far enough back, all humans share the same ancestors.
experiments.safety: Keep rice away from very small children.

experiments.title: The chore survey
experiments.question: Who does the work in our home?
need: a chart with days across the top and jobs down the side (cooking, washing up, sweeping, clothes, shopping, caring for children or elders, fetching water, paid work outside)
a pen kept by the chart
steps: Stick the chart on the fridge or wall on Day 1.
Each time someone does a job, they write their initial and roughly how many minutes.
Keep it going until Day 6.
Add up the minutes for each person.
Draw a bar chart.
experiments.predict: Ask everyone at home to guess who does the most work before you start.
experiments.observe: In many homes, one or two people (often women) do most of the cooking, cleaning and caring, while the work of paid jobs is more visible.
experiments.why: Care work keeps every family alive, but because it is unpaid and happens every day, it is often not noticed or counted. Measuring it is the first step to sharing it fairly. Children can share it too.
experiments.time: 5 min on Day 1, a minute a day after, 12 min on Day 6

activities.title: Our family tree
need: a phone to call an elder
steps: Draw a trunk with your child's name.
Draw two branches for parents (or the people who raise them), then grandparents above them.
Add brothers, sisters, aunts, uncles and cousins.
Write the kinship word your family uses for each person.
Add each person's birthplace and one thing they love.
Call an elder to fill in great-grandparents if anyone remembers them.
activities.outcome: A three- or four-generation family tree with kinship words and places.

activities.title: Then-and-now interview with an elder
need: paper or a phone to record
steps: Write the questions on a card before you start.
Ask: where did you grow up, how many people lived in your home, what did you eat, how did you go to school, what did children do at home?
Ask: what is better now? What was better then?
Ask: what is one thing you want me to remember?
Write or record the answers and thank them.
activities.outcome: A short written or recorded interview to keep in the family book.

voices.who: Douglas Rohde, Steve Olson and Joseph Chang, USA (published in Nature, 2004)
voices.idea: Using computer models of how people have moved and had children over thousands of years, they estimated that the most recent person who is an ancestor of every human alive today may have lived only a few thousand years ago. A few thousand years further back, every person alive was either an ancestor of everyone living now, or of no one.
voices.then: Many people were surprised, because we usually think of family trees as separate. Others pointed out that islands and isolated groups could push the dates further back.
voices.now: The mathematics is accepted: family trees must join, and all humans share recent common ancestors. The exact dates are uncertain and depend on how much people moved and mixed, so they are still debated.
voices.ask: If every person alive shares ancestors who lived only a few thousand years ago, what does that mean for the way people divide themselves into 'us' and 'them'?

voices.who: Cynthia Moss (born 1940), USA, working in Amboseli, Kenya
voices.idea: Since 1972 Moss and her team in the Amboseli Elephant Research Project have followed the same elephant families, generation after generation. They found that elephant families are led by the oldest female, the matriarch, and that calves are cared for by many females. With Karen McComb and others, they showed in 2001 that families led by older matriarchs are better at telling the calls of friendly families from the calls of strangers. Later work showed that older matriarchs also judge the danger from lions better, because they have learned more in their long lives.
voices.then: Early elephant studies paid most attention to big males and their tusks. Moss's patient, decades-long watching of females and families changed the picture.
voices.now: It is accepted: elephant families are matriarchal, and old females carry knowledge that helps everyone survive. Elephants with old matriarchs killed by poachers can lose that knowledge.
voices.ask: Why might an elephant family need its oldest member most of all? Who carries that kind of knowledge in a human family?

voices.idea: In her book Mothers and Others (2009), Hrdy argued that humans are 'cooperative breeders': unlike chimpanzee mothers, who care for their babies almost alone, human mothers have always needed help from grandmothers, fathers, older children and others. She suggests this is why humans became so good at understanding what others think and feel.
voices.then: Many scientists had assumed that a mother alone, or a mother and father, raised human children. Her idea challenged that.
voices.now: Most scientists agree that human children have always been raised with help from many people. Whether this is the main reason humans became so good at understanding each other is still debated.
voices.ask: How could scientists find out whether children in the past were raised by many people? What evidence would they look for?

voices.idea: In her book If Women Counted (1988), Waring showed that the way countries measure their economy leaves out unpaid work done at home, such as cooking, cleaning, caring for children and elders, and fetching water, most of which is done by women. So the work that keeps families alive appears to be worth nothing.
voices.then: Many economists said this kind of work was too hard to measure. Waring's work helped persuade countries to run time-use surveys, which measure how people spend their day.
voices.now: It is accepted that unpaid care work is huge and mostly done by women; India's first national Time Use Survey (2019) found women spending about five hours a day on it and men about one and a half. How it should be counted and valued is still debated.
voices.ask: If cooking at home were paid like cooking in a restaurant, would people value it more? Is everything valuable something that should have a price?

project.title: Our family book
steps: Make the handprint cover on Day 1.
Add the family tree with kinship words (Day 2) and the trait survey (Day 3).
Add the doubling ancestors numbers and the two joining trees (Day 4).
Add the 'who helped raise me' list (Day 5) and the chore bar chart (Day 6).
Add the elder's interview (Day 7).
Bind the book and present it on Day 9.
project.outcome: A family book with a handprint cover, family tree, trait survey, chore chart and an elder's memories, to keep and add to.

game.title: Relation Rummy
rules: Cut out the cards. Each set has three cards: the relation, its word in one language, and its word in another.
Shuffle and deal 5 cards to each player. Put the rest face down as the pile.
On your turn, take a card from the pile, then throw one away face up.
When you have a set of three that match (the same relation), lay it down and say the relation aloud.
The first player to lay down two sets wins. Then everyone says what they call that relative at home.

big: What makes someone family: blood, law, living together, or love?
If all humans share ancestors, are all humans one family?
Is work that nobody pays for still work? Is it worth less?
Which things should a family pass on to its children, and which should children be free to change?
Can an animal, a tree or a place be part of your family?

challenge.q: People say 'blood is thicker than water': family by birth matters most. Is that true?
challenge.hint: Genes are only part of what a family passes on. Studies of adopted children show they take on a great deal from the families who raise them: language, values, habits, and much of how they feel about themselves. Many people also have 'chosen family'. Ask: in your own life, who has been most like family to you, and why?

challenge.q: A popular picture shows early humans as a man hunting while a woman waits in the cave with the baby. Is that how human children were raised?
challenge.hint: Studies of present-day hunter-gatherer peoples, such as the Hadza of Tanzania, show grandmothers, older children, fathers and others all helping to feed and carry babies, and women gathering much of the food; some research suggests women in many such groups also hunted. Exactly how life was in the deep past is still debated. Ask: who might have drawn the old picture, and what did they leave out?

challenge.q: Some people say 'a family needs one head who decides everything'. Do other animals agree?
challenge.hint: Families and groups are run in many ways. Elephant families follow the experience of an old female; many birds share decisions between parents; honeybee swarms choose a new home by something like a vote among scouts. Human families also make decisions in many ways. Ask: how are decisions made in your family? Who gets a say?

perspectives.who: A child in an adoptive family
perspectives.view: Many adopted children say their family is just their family, and they don't think about genes at all. Some want to know about their birth parents; some don't. Ask: why should every child get to decide for themselves how they feel about their own story?
A calf grows up surrounded by her mother, aunts, sisters and cousins, and follows her grandmother's memory to water. Ask: what would you learn if your grandmother led your family on every journey?

perspectives.who: A domestic worker who cares for another family's children
perspectives.view: Many children in Indian cities are partly raised by an akka, didi, ayah or nanny, who may also have her own children at home being looked after by someone else. Ask: is she part of the family she works for? What does she need?
Grandparents carry the family's memories, recipes, songs and games. Ask: what would be lost if no one asked them about their childhood?

story.title: Where My Tree Begins
text: The worksheet had a picture of a tree on it, a big one with lots of empty boxes on the branches, and at the top it said, in Ma'am's neat handwriting: My Family Tree. Fill in at least three generations. Due Monday.

Everyone else in Class 3 thought it was easy. Rehaan said he had already done his and that his great-grandfather was a famous wrestler in Kolhapur. Meenakshi had a photo of her great-great-grandmother in a nine-yard madisar sari. I folded my worksheet into a small square and put it at the bottom of my bag.

I am Tara. I was adopted when I was eleven months old. I know because Amma and Appa have always told me, ever since I can remember, the story of the day they came to the home in Chennai where I was, and how I grabbed Appa's spectacles off his nose and wouldn't give them back. I like that story. But the worksheet tree had roots drawn at the bottom, thick brown roots going down into the ground, and I didn't know what to write there.

On Saturday my cousin Kavya came to stay. Kavya Akka is fifteen and does maths for fun, which I think is strange, but she is also the only person who will play carrom with me for two hours without getting bored. She found the worksheet when she was looking for a pencil in my bag.
“Oh, this is fun,” she said, unfolding it on the floor. “Let's do it.”
“I can't,” I said.
She looked at me. Then she looked at the roots at the bottom of the tree. Kavya Akka is clever in more than maths.
“Okay,” she said. “Let's do it a different way. Get the rice.”
“The rice?”
“The rice. From the kitchen. Uncooked.”
I brought the steel dabba. She took out one grain and put it on the floor. “That's you.”
Then she put down two grains above it. “Everybody has two birth parents. Even you. Even me. Even the Prime Minister.”

Above that she put four. “Four grandparents.” Then eight. “Eight great-grandparents.” Then sixteen, and I helped count. Then thirty-two, which took a while. Then sixty-four, and the rice was getting all over the floor, and Amma called from the kitchen asking what we were doing with her rice.
“Maths!” Kavya Akka called back.

We stopped at sixty-four because we were running out of floor. Kavya Akka got out her phone and opened the calculator. “Every time you go back one generation, it doubles. So let's keep going.” She pressed the buttons. “Ten generations: one thousand and twenty-four. Twenty generations: about a million. Thirty generations, that's about seven or eight hundred years ago: more than a billion.”
“A billion grandparents?”
“Places for grandparents. Here's the thing.” She leaned forward. “Eight hundred years ago, there weren't a billion people in the whole world. Not even close. So how can you have a billion ancestors?”
I thought about it. The rice on the floor looked like a tree upside down, spreading wider and wider.
“They have to be the same people,” I said slowly. “Some of them are in lots of the boxes.”

“Yes!” Kavya Akka looked as happy as if I had won at carrom. “Your great-great-great-whatever on one side is also your great-great-great-whatever on another side. The branches cross. They join up. And it's not just your tree. Mine too. Everybody's. Go back far enough and everybody's trees run into each other. Scientists have worked it out with computers. Go back a few thousand years, and some of the people alive then are ancestors of everybody alive now. Everybody. You, me, Rehaan and his wrestler, the Prime Minister, a girl in Brazil.”
I looked at the rice for a long time.
“So my roots,” I said, “are the same as everyone's roots.”

“Your roots are everyone's roots,” said Kavya Akka. “You just don't know their names yet. Nobody does, after a few generations. Rehaan doesn't know the name of his great-great-great-great-grandmother either.”
Then Amma came in, and saw the rice, and opened her mouth to say something, and then she saw my face and shut it again and sat down on the floor with us.

On Monday I handed in my tree. In the top branches I wrote Amma and Appa, and Paati and Thatha, and Ammamma, who lives in Madurai, and Kavya Akka on a little side branch with a drawing of a carrom board. Lower down, near the trunk, I wrote my own name.
And at the bottom, in the roots, where the worksheet wanted names, I glued rice. Sixty-four grains, in a fan, spreading out and out until they went off the edge of the paper.
Ma'am asked me what the rice was.
“Everybody,” I said.
story.epiphany: Everyone has two birth parents, four grandparents, eight great-grandparents: the places in a family tree double each generation, so within about thirty generations they outnumber all the people who were alive. The same ancestors must fill many places, so family trees join, and far enough back all humans share ancestors. The turn comes when Tara realises her 'missing' roots are everyone's roots. Underneath: a family is made by care (Amma, Appa, Kavya Akka), and its roots are shared by all.
ask: Why did Tara fold the worksheet and hide it?
Why did the rice keep doubling? What did Tara work out about the billion places?
What did Kavya Akka mean when she said 'Your roots are everyone's roots'?
Why do you think Amma sat down on the floor instead of scolding them about the rice?
Who is in Tara's family? Who is in yours?

ideas.idea: A family is made of care, in many shapes.
ideas.more: Joint, nuclear, single-parent, adoptive, foster, grandparent-led and chosen families all do the same thing: they belong to and look after each other. Show it with the handprint: every hand different, all on one sheet.

ideas.idea: Far enough back, every family tree joins: all humans are relatives.
ideas.more: Ancestors double every generation, so the same people must fill many places. Within a few thousand years, everyone alive shares ancestors. Show it with the rice.

ideas.idea: Children have always been raised by many hands.
ideas.more: Elephant aunts, meerkat helpers, grandmothers, older cousins, neighbours, teachers. No mother or father has ever done it alone, and the work of caring, often unpaid and unseen, holds every family up.

unknowns: Exactly when did the most recent common ancestor of all living humans live? Estimates range over thousands of years, and nobody knows for sure.
How much of who we are comes from genes and how much from the family and world we grow up in? Scientists agree it is both, tangled together, but still argue about the details for most traits.

Why do grandmothers in humans, and in a few other animals such as killer whales, live so long after they stop having babies? Scientists think helping their grandchildren survive is part of the answer, but it is still debated.

books.title: The Family Book
books.author: Todd Parr
books.why: Bright, simple pictures of many shapes of family, all with something in common.

books.title: A Chair for My Mother
books.author: Vera B. Williams
books.why: A girl, her mother and grandmother save coins in a jar for a new chair after a fire, helped by their neighbours. About family, work and community.

books.title: Tell Me Again About the Night I Was Born
books.author: Jamie Lee Curtis
books.why: An adopted girl asks her parents to tell her favourite story: the night she joined her family.

books.title: Elephant Memories: Thirteen Years in the Life of an Elephant Family
books.author: Cynthia Moss
books.why: The scientist's own account of following one elephant family in Amboseli. Read aloud a few passages about the matriarch.

check.q: Name four shapes of family. What do they all share?
check.a: Any four of joint, nuclear, single-parent, adoptive, foster, grandparent-led, chosen; they all care for and belong to each other.

check.q: What do you call your father's sister and your mother's sister in your language?
check.a: For example athai, atte, atta, bua or pishi for a father's sister, and chithi, pinni, chikkamma, mausi or mashi for a mother's sister.

check.q: Give one feature passed on through genes and one that is learned.
check.a: For example, curly hair (genes) and speaking Malayalam (learned).

check.q: How many great-great-grandparents does a person have, and why do everyone's family trees join?
check.a: Sixteen. Ancestors double each generation until there are more places than people who lived, so the same ancestors fill many places and trees join.

check.q: Who leads an elephant family, and why does it matter?
check.a: The oldest female, the matriarch; her memory and experience help the family find water and avoid danger.

check.q: What did the chore survey show, and why does unpaid work matter?
check.a: Your own result; unpaid cooking, cleaning and caring keeps every family alive but is often unseen and unevenly shared.

check.q: Name three things every child has a right to.
check.a: For example: food, a safe home, health care, love, schooling (free from 6 to 14 in India), play, being listened to.

check.q: What did Tara glue in the roots of her tree, and why?
check.a: Rice grains spreading out, because her roots, like everyone's, are shared by everybody.
